entries.meaning: Possibly olive tree
entries.note: A Latin olive connection is one explanation; a Germanic origin is also possible.

entries.meaning: Associated with the olive
entries.note: Its spelling may come from Oliva, Oliver, or the Latin word for olive.

entries.meaning: Possibly friend of deer
entries.note: This is one proposed Irish derivation. Germanic origins have also been suggested.

entries.meaning: By proprialization of oak + -land, as likewise with Oakwood from oakwood.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: A variant of Oakland or Oaklyn.
entries.note: A unisex given name.

entries.meaning: From Old English Āclēa, from āc (“oak”) + lēah (“woodland clearing, glade”), thus a clearing in an oak forest; equivalent to oak + -ley (“lea”). Compare Ackley, Akeley and Oakleigh, which have the same origin.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: A variant of Oakley with -lyn.
entries.note: A unisex given name.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew עובדיה (Ovadya, “servant of Yahweh”); comparable to Arabic عبد اللّٰه (ʕabd-allah, “servant of God”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew, of biblical origin.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew אובד or עוֹבֵד (Oved, “servant”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew of biblical origin.

entries.meaning: From ocean (“sea”), inspired by the fashionable French female name Océane.
entries.note: A female given name from English, of modern usage.

entries.meaning: From Latin Octāvia, feminine form of the gens name Octāvius, from octavus (“the eighth”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, in quiet use since the Middle Ages.

entries.meaning: From Latin Octavianus, derivative of Octāvius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, notably borne by Augustus (Caesar) between 44 and 27 BCE

entries.meaning: From Latin Octāvius, name of a Roman gens.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, in occasional use.

entries.meaning: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French octobre, from Latin Octōber (“eighth month”), from Latin octō (“eight”), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw (“twice four”); + Latin -ber, from -bris, an adjectival suffix; October was the eighth month in the Roman calendar.
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the month name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Oda.
entries.note: A female given name in German.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic عُدَي (ʕuday).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: English surname, from the Middle English name Ode, either from Anglo-Norman Ode (see Oates) or from Old English Odda, Old Norse Oddr, or a conflation of all. Compare Oddy.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Separate origins as diminutives of British name Odell and Germanic name Odin; later used as nickname for additional given names.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given names Odell, Odin, Ogilvie, Otis, Odysseus, Odicea, Odoardo, and Odunayo, also used as a formal given name.

entries.meaning: From Latin Otho.
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage.

entries.meaning: From Greek Οδυσσέα (Odysséa), feminine of Οδυσσέας (Odysséas).
entries.note: A female given name from Greek, of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ὀδυσσεύς (Odusseús). Doublet of Ulysses.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Oenōnē, from Ancient Greek Οἰνώνη (Oinṓnē).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew עֹפֶר (“fawn”).
entries.note: A male given name of Hebrew origin.

entries.meaning: Places in England, from Old English āc (“oak”) + denu (“valley”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of occasional usage.

entries.meaning: From Macedonian Огнен (Ognen), from огнен (ognen).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Macedonian male given name Огнен (Ognen)

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Yoruba Ògún.
entries.note: A male given name from Yoruba.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Yoruba Ọládípọ̀
entries.note: A male given name from Yoruba

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Danish Ole.
entries.note: A male given name from Danish.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Russian Оле́г (Olég), a Varangian name, ultimately from Old Norse Helgi (“holy, sacred or blessed”). Cognate to modern Scandinavian Helge.
entries.note: A male given name from the Slavic languages.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Ukrainian Олекса́ндер (Oleksánder).
entries.note: A male given name from Ukrainian, equivalent to English Alexander.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ukrainian Олекса́ндра (Oleksándra).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Ukrainian female given name Олекса́ндра (Oleksándra)

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ukrainian Оле́на (Oléna).
entries.note: A female given name from Ukrainian, equivalent to English Helen.

entries.meaning: From Russian and Ukrainian Олеся (Olesja).
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Aleksandra /Oleksandra, equivalent to English Alexis of Russian and Ukrainian usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed in the 19th century from Old East Slavic О́льга (Ólĭga), name of a Kievan knyaginya (Saint Olga of Kiev), a medieval form of Helga, Old Norse heilagr (“holy; inviolable, sacred”). Doublet of Helga.
entries.note: A female given name from Russian, Ukrainian, or Belarusian.

entries.meaning: Doublet of Helga.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Ukrainian female given name О́льга (Ólʹha)

entries.meaning: Medieval form of the Latin saint's name Oliva "olive"; revived in the 19th century when flower and plant names became fashionable. The surname is topographical, often representing an Anglicization of continental European surnames such as Spanish Oliva.
entries.note: A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from French Olivier. Doublet of Oliver.
entries.note: A male given name from French, equivalent to English Oliver.

entries.meaning: From Germanic, from Latin olivarius (“olive tree”) (from oliva (“olive”)), and from Welsh.
entries.note: A unisex given name. A diminutive of the male given name Oliver, from French [in turn from Latin, in turn from Germanic].

entries.meaning: From Welsh Olwen.
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh from Welsh legend, specifically The Mabinogion.

entries.meaning: From Welsh ol (“footprint”) and gwen (“fair, white”).
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh, variant of Olwen.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπία (Olumpía), from Ὄλυμπος (Ólumpos, “Olympus”).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek; quite rare in English.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ὀλυμπιάς (Olumpiás).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage.

entries.meaning: Coined as a feminine equivalent of Omar.
entries.note: A female given name

entries.meaning: From Arabic عُمَر (ʕumar). Doublet of Umar.
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic عمري. The surname is predominantly found in Tanzania.
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: From Persian امید (omid).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Persian male given name امید (omid).

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Naomi.

entries.meaning: From an ancient Sanskrit name ओंकार (oṃkāra, “om, aum”) adopted by Hindus which translated means “the primordial sound from which the universe was manifest,” shortened to ॐ (oṃ).
entries.note: A male given name from India.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew אוֹנָן (onán).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Popularized by Trinididian-American rapper Onika Tanya Maraj-Petty (Nicki Minaj), born 1982.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Ondeslow, Ondeslowe, Ondeslawe, Andeslawe, Hundeslawe, Hundreslawe, Andreslawe, from Old English *Andrǣd (a male given name) + hlāw, hlǣw (“hill”) (literally, "Ander's hill").
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Irish Úna; doublet of Una.
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Variant spelling of Oona, Una, Anglicized from Irish Úna.
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit ऊर्जा (ūrjā, “power, energy”).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Ofelia, coined by the poet Jacopo Sannazaro in his poem Arcadia (1504), probably from the Ancient Greek ὠφέλειᾰ (ōphéleiă, “help, aid, succour”). The name was used by William Shakespeare for the daugher of Polonius and ill-fated love interest of Hamlet. The moon (of Uranus) is named after this character. Doublet of anopheles
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Ophelia + -ana.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew אוֹפִיר. Mentioned as a place in the Bible; modern scholars have been unable to determine where it was located.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Oprah Winfrey, a very influential talk show host, originally named Orpah after the Biblical figure, via metathesis.
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew, of modern usage, variant of Orpah.

entries.meaning: * (given name): First appeared in the 19th century when similar sounding names like Cora, Dora and Nora were in fashion. Possibly shortened from Aurelia, sometimes spelled Ora Lee, or, Aura Lea, in the American civil war song. * (Italian commune): Borrowed from Italian Ora
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Aurelia, from Latin, variant of Aura. Mainly used in the U.S.A. in the latter half of the 19th century.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Latin Aurelius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin of American usage

entries.meaning: Anglicized from Old Irish saints' name Odrán, diminutive of odur (“dun, sallow”) (compare Irish Odhrán).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Italian Orchidea, from orchidea (“orchid”).
entries.note: A female given name from Italian [in turn from Latin], of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hebrew אורן (“pine tree”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew, probably from the Bible (1 Chronicles 2:25).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Late Latin Ōrigenēs, from Koine Greek Ὠριγένης (Ōrigénēs), probably ultimately from Ὧρος (Hôros, “Horus”) + -γενής (-genḗs, “born of”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage, notably borne by Origen of Alexandria, an early Church Father.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Orioun, from Latin Ōrīōn, from Ancient Greek Ὠρίων (Ōríōn), speculatively from Akkadian 𒌋𒊒𒀭𒈾 (Uru-anna, “heaven's light”), though without any firm evidence.
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek of modern usage.

entries.meaning: Anglicized version of Irish Órfhlaith (“golden princess”), from ór (“gold”) + flaith (“princess”).
entries.note: A female given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: From Italian Orlando (“Roland”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Hrōþiland. The city in Florida has gone by the name since 1857, perhaps in honor of the soldier Orlando Reeves, whom the Seminoles killed there in 1835. Previously, it had been settled in 1844 as Jernigan. Doublet of Roland.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew עׇרְפָּה (orpá, “neck”).
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Ὀρφεύς (Orpheús), built from an uncertain root with the -εύς (-eús) suffix. Perhaps root-cognate to Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “orphan”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: English surname from a vernacular form of the personal name Horace.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Apparently a patronymic surname from Orris + -son.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Yoruba Ọ̀rúnmìlà.
entries.note: A male given name from Yoruba.

entries.meaning: Invented by Fanny Burney for the hero of her novel Evelina. It has been suggested that it is based on the very old Welsh forename of Eurfyl, meaning 'gold'.
entries.note: A male given name originating as a coinage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic أُسَامَة (ʔusāma).
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Japanese おさむ (Osamu).
entries.note: A male given name from Japanese.

entries.meaning: Variant of Osborne.
entries.note: An English surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From a medieval given name influenced by, or possibly derived from, Old Norse Ásbjǫrn, from áss (“god”) + bjǫrn (“bear”). Compare also Old English Ōsbeorn. Components related to Æsir and bear respectively.
entries.note: An English surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: From Irish Oisín.
entries.note: A male given name from Irish.

entries.meaning: Inherited from Middle English, from Old Norse Ásmundr, from áss (“a god”) + mund (“protection, hand”).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, variant of Osmond, rare in English.

entries.meaning: Old Norse Ásmundr, from áss (“a god”) + mund (“protection, hand”). Later merged with a Norman French Osmond, Osmont, Omont from the same Old Norse root. Cognate with native Old English Ōsmund.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages, rare in English.

entries.meaning: An anglicisation, made known by James Macpherson, of Irish Oisín, diminutive form of os (“deer”).
entries.note: A male given name from Irish; rather rare in the Anglo-Saxon world.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Ukrainian Оста́п (Ostáp), ultimately from Ancient Greek Εὐστάθιος (Eustáthios). Doublet of Eustace.
entries.note: A transliteration of the Russian or Ukrainian male given name Оста́п (Ostáp).

entries.meaning: Inherited from Old English Oswine, from ōs (“god, deity”) + wine (“friend”).
entries.note: A male given name from Old English. Oswine of Deira, 7th century King of Deira.

entries.meaning: From Old Norse Othorere, originating during the Viking occupation of England.
entries.note: A male given name from Old Norse, of rare usage, used as an aristocratic heritage familial given name.

entries.meaning: From Biblical Hebrew עָתְנִיאֵל (ʿOṯnīʾēl), of uncertain meaning but at any rate ending in אֵל (ʾēl, “God”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: A patronymic surname derived from Middle English genitive case of the Germanic given name Ote, Ode, cognate to modern Otto.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name, notably of the American revolutionary hero James Otis and the innovator and industrialist Elisha Otis.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Ottilie.
entries.note: A female given name from German.

entries.meaning: From Ottilie + -ine.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Otto, from Old High German, short form of compound names (such as Otachar, Ottokar) beginning with Proto-West Germanic *aud, from Proto-Germanic *audaz (“wealth, riches”) (cognate of English Ed- in Edgar, Edmund, Edward, Edith, etc.).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Ottokar.
entries.note: A male given name from German.

entries.meaning: From a modified version of Ottilie, perhaps after Otto, + -ine.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: From Latin Ovidius, name of a Roman gens.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin of mainly historic use.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Welsh Owain. Doublet of Owen.
entries.note: A male given name from Welsh, equivalent to English Owen.

entries.meaning: From various origins. See below
entries.note: A male given name. A male given name from Welsh, an anglicization of Welsh Owain.

entries.meaning: From Owen + -s (patronymic suffix).
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Russian Оюб (Ojub).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Russian male given name Оюб (Ojub)

entries.meaning: Abbreviations.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Diminutive forms, + -ie.
entries.note: A male given name. A diminutive of the male given name Oswald.

entries.meaning: Clippings + -y
entries.note: A male given name.
